passage: Indu, come, let me tell you about the launch that taught me to sort my worries. I'm Minakshi, and I was a new manager then. We ran a pre-mortem, and the board filled with thirty-odd ideas: printers, pigeons on the roof, a vendor's mood. Next morning I looked at it and my stomach dropped; it was a wall of worry and I couldn't act on any of it. So I sat with a pen and marked each idea twice: how likely, and how costly. Only three scored high on both: the payment gateway going down, our one trained person falling ill, and stock arriving late. For those I planned backups. The rest I decided to live with. A pigeon did cause a hiccup, and we laughed. The gateway did stumble, and the backup carried us.

qa.a: Minakshi kept the payment gateway going down, the one trained person falling ill, and stock arriving late.

qa.q: Which choice turned the list from a wall of worry into a plan, and why?
qa.a: Marking each idea for how likely and how costly it was, and keeping only those high on both, gave backups for the few risks that mattered.

qa.q: How might the team have felt when the gateway stumbled and the backup carried them?
qa.a: They were probably relieved and reassured that the plan had worked, after having already laughed at the pigeon hiccup.

The steel plant visit had been cancelled at the last minute, so Arohi had only the train back to Kolkata to fix the rollout plan. Four hours, patchy signal, and the go-live was Monday.
On her laptop was the list from the team's pre-mortem: twenty-seven ways the new inventory system could fail. Darshan had typed it up faithfully. Reading it now, she saw the trouble. "Staff forget passwords" sat next to "server room floods". Everything had the same bold font.
She added two columns, likely and costly, and scored each from one to three. Three rose to the top: warehouse scanners not paired, night-shift staff untrained, old stock codes not matching.
She messaged Darshan when the signal came back. "Top three only. Pair scanners Friday, train night shift Saturday, map codes Sunday. The rest we accept and watch."

qa.q: How many ways to fail were on the pre-mortem list?
qa.a: The list had twenty-seven ways the new inventory system could fail.

qa.q: What did Arohi feel when she saw every risk in the same bold font?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and frustrated, because the list was unfocused and gave small risks the same weight as serious ones.

qa.q: What would you add to Arohi's plan for the risks she accepted?
qa.a: A simple weekly check on the accepted risks would help, so if one becomes more likely it can move into the top group.

qa.q: How might Darshan see the new message after typing the long list?
qa.a: Darshan may feel relieved to have three clear jobs with dates instead of twenty-seven worries, though perhaps unsure about leaving the rest.

grounding: It shows a manager seeing an unfocused pre-mortem list, keeping the three likely and costly risks, planning for those and accepting the rest.

Anjali had pinned the pre-mortem sheet to the glass wall of the Gurugram office on Tuesday. By Thursday it had forty sticky notes and nobody was doing anything about any of them.
"We're drowning," Chetan said, standing beside her with his coffee.
She pulled all the notes off and laid them on the table. "Two questions for each. Will it probably happen? Would it really hurt?"
They sorted for an hour. Most notes landed in "unlikely" or "annoying but small." Three stayed in the corner that was both: the vendor delivering late, the new hire not trained before launch, and the data migration failing halfway.
Anjali wrote a plan for each on a single page. A backup vendor. A training week. A test migration on Sunday. She stuck the other thirty-seven notes in an envelope labelled "accepted".
Chetan grinned. "That envelope is my favourite thing this month."

qa.q: How many notes went into the envelope labelled accepted?
qa.a: The other thirty-seven notes went into the envelope.

qa.q: Why did Anjali pull all the notes off the wall?
qa.a: She was frustrated that forty notes had led to no action, and wanted to sort them so the team could focus.

qa.q: What else could Anjali do with the accepted envelope, and why?
qa.a: She could reopen it once a month, since some small risks may grow as the launch gets closer.

qa.q: How does Chetan feel about the new one-page plan?
qa.a: Chetan is relieved and amused, calling the envelope his favourite thing this month after saying the team was drowning. 😄

grounding: It shows a manager narrowing a sprawling pre-mortem to the three risks that are likely and costly, planning for them and accepting the rest.
